Zack Wheeler is back, but questions remain for Phillies with 10 games left

Zack Wheeler is back, but questions remain for Phillies with 10 games left

September 17, 2026 | 10:53 AM EDT
Bob Cooney

A Decrease font size. A Reset font size. A Increase font size.

WASHINGTON — Make it four in a row for Phillies ace Zack Wheeler, and it couldn’t be happening at a better time.

Wheeler had his fourth consecutive stellar outing following a four-game struggle to carry the Phillies to a 3-0 win over the Washington Nationals. Wheeler has talked recently of the slight, yet necessary adjustments he had to make in order for the turnaround, and he has done it to perfection of late. His seven-inning stint — in which he allowed just four hits, struck out five and issued just one walk Wednesday — lended further proof. And so did him finishing the night with a strikeout on a 97 mph fastball on his 91st and final pitch.

“I know it’s probably my last inning so just trying to really execute that pitch and put everything behind it that I could,” Wheeler said. “I just tried to reach back and execute that pitch and I was able to.

“There’s a game plan coming in knowing that these guys are super aggressive. They’re swinging at the first pitch a lot, so I threw a lot of first pitch balls. That was kind of on purpose just to see if I could get weak contact, if I was going in and try to throw off the plate, if I was going away, trying to make them chase a ball or two off the plate. A couple there, early, got back over the middle that they hit up the middle, line drives early. But for the most part, I was trying to throw outside the zone, as weird as that sounds, just to try to use their aggressiveness against them.”

That’s how back Wheeler is. No longer is it just trying to find his location and fix his mechanics, now it’s executing exactly what his game plan is.

“I thought he was good,” said interim manager Don Mattingly. “Kind of on the attack, pretty much no real stressful innings. For the most part, kind of kept them in check all night. 

“It’s four in a row now that he’s been positive starts. We tried to keep his pitch count down tonight. We wanted to keep him around 90 tonight and not push him any further. He made it easy to go back out there (for the seventh).”

Easy because his pitcher was so good. Not so easy that the offense could only muster three runs on the 13 walks the six Nationals pitchers issued.

“It’s pretty amazing, 13 walks is a lot of walks,” said Mattingly. “I look at it as we won tonight. That’s how I look at it. No matter how we do it, we got a win. That’s what matters at the end of the day. Obviously, you have chances to do more. We weren’t able to do that. But, we’ll take the W, take the approach and go from there.”

The number of factors that have to get better, stay the same or just happen for the Phillies as they stroll towards the final 10 games of the season after Wednesday’s win are almost too long to list. There are starting pitching woes that include an injury and some struggles. A plan of how to approach at-bats in the month of August seems to have waned a bit. The bullpen is still mostly an audition of who wants high-leverage roles, and there is the fact the offense barely did enough for Wheeler on Wednesday to get him the win.

And then there is Brandon Marsh. The outfielder who was an All-Star starter just a couple of months ago and was hovering near the top of the National League in batting average, now has morphed into a weak-hitting, platoon outfielder who hasn’t given Mattingly any reason to even flirt with the idea of having him in the lineup against a left-handed starter.

To his credit, the affable Marsh doesn’t let on of his struggles on the field since reaching the highest point of his career during the Midsummer Classic in Philadelphia. He is the lead cheerleader in the dugout, whether it’s for his replacement or anyone else. He is the type of guy every team in every sport would want in the locker room. But an improvement on his struggles now wouldn’t just be a nice thing to see for a good teammate, it is almost imperative in order for the Phillies to reach their goals.

“I just think they made an adjustment to him and we’ve got to make (adjustments) back, and we haven’t been able to do that, in general,” said Mattingly.

“Marsh is sitting back there at some point and they’re probably not doing a ton of homework on him and they’re attacking him or whatever. He gets aggressive, or starts being aggressive and he’s doing his damage, he’s getting hits. All of the sudden he’s hitting .330 and he’s on the All-Star team and it’s like, ‘Maybe we ought to do a little more work on this guy.’ You see adjustments all the time and I think that’s what’s happened, basically. At some point, he’s aggressive and they’re going to be less likely to throw strikes and get him to chase a little bit more. And then we have to make the adjustment to back down the aggression. Be aggressive on your swing, but it doesn’t mean you swing at everything.”

Marsh has done a little bit of that through a slump that has him hitting .179 since the All-Star Game. His outs, once loud and full of possibilities, are now mostly the soft type. You expect a breakout at any time, like on Wednesday when the Phillies had the bases loaded with two outs against the Nationals. The team had already scored two runs on wild Washington pitching, and it just felt like the right spot. Instead he hit a lazy fly to left on a 1-0 count that ended the inning. He is now hitless in his last 13 at-bats.

On the other side of that, Mattingly has no concerns when it comes to second baseman Luis Arraez, who is trying to collect his fourth batting title, though he really hasn’t hit his stride with the Phillies just yet. Mattingly sees it as if the second baseman just needs to relax and be who he’s been at the plate for his career. Arraez seems to be hitting a hot spot as he reached base seven times in his nine plate appearances in the two games in Washington.

“He’s fine,” Mattingly said. “I think sometimes, what I see with Luis, is that situation with a guy on third it’s kind of like a sacrifice fly situation, but to me, Luis should just hit. Just get his hits. If he has to hit the ball, it depends on who’s on third base and did he hit it far enough? There’s times you want him to hit the ball on the right side, you’ve got guys on second and third, nobody out and they’re playing back and they’re going to give us a run and let us move the runner, then I’m hoping he hits the ball on the ground on the right side.

“What I have seen with the third base situation is him trying to hit a sac fly. Sometimes he’s real aggressive. Sometimes he’s not aggressive at all. Him and I talked yesterday. He’ maybe, historically, one of the best guys ever with men in scoring position. So I don’t think he’s trying to hit homers or fly balls. I just think he’s hitting. I encourage him just to be himself and just hit. Don’t try to do too much or try to do one specific thing. Just take his rips.”
